text: A table has DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 30 on Enterprise Edition. An engineer accidentally deletes the table. How long can they use UNDROP TABLE to restore it?

options.A: 7 days (Fail-safe period)
options.B: 30 days — the table's Time Travel retention period
options.C: 37 days (30 Time Travel + 7 Fail-safe)
options.D: 90 days (maximum Enterprise retention)

explanation: UNDROP works during the Time Travel retention period (30 days here). After Time Travel expires, data moves to Fail-safe (7 days) which is only accessible by Snowflake Support — NOT via UNDROP.

text: A permanent table has 10-day Time Travel and 7-day Fail-safe. What is the TOTAL data protection window?

options.A: 10 days
options.B: 7 days
options.C: 17 days (10 Time Travel + 7 Fail-safe)
options.D: 90 days

explanation: Total protection = Time Travel + Fail-safe. For permanent tables: retention days (user-accessible) + 7 days Fail-safe (Snowflake Support only). 10 + 7 = 17 days.

text: Can a user directly recover data from Fail-safe using UNDROP or Time Travel queries?

options.A: Yes — UNDROP works during both Time Travel and Fail-safe
options.B: No — Fail-safe data is ONLY recoverable by Snowflake Support. Users cannot access it.
options.C: Yes, but only with ACCOUNTADMIN role
options.D: Yes, using AT(OFFSET => -failsafe_days)

explanation: Fail-safe is NOT user-accessible. Only Snowflake Support can attempt recovery from Fail-safe on a best-effort basis. UNDROP and AT/BEFORE only work during Time Travel. This is one of the most tested distinctions on the exam.

text: What is the Fail-safe period for transient tables?

options.A: 7 days (same as permanent tables)
options.B: 1 day
options.C: 0 days — transient tables have NO Fail-safe
options.D: Depends on the edition

explanation: Transient and temporary tables have 0 days of Fail-safe. This reduces storage costs but means data is permanently lost after Time Travel expires (0-1 day max).

text: An engineer queries SELECT * FROM orders AT(OFFSET => -300). What point in time does this reference?

options.A: 300 minutes ago
options.B: 300 seconds (5 minutes) ago
options.C: 300 rows back
options.D: The 300th micro-partition

explanation: AT(OFFSET => -n) specifies n SECONDS ago (not minutes, not rows). -300 = 300 seconds = 5 minutes ago. This is a common exam trap — always think in seconds for OFFSET.

text: A database has DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 10. A table within it does NOT have an explicit retention set. What is the table's effective retention?

options.A: 0 days (default when not explicitly set)
options.B: 1 day (system default)
options.C: 10 days — inherited from the parent database
options.D: 90 days (Enterprise maximum)

explanation: Tables inherit retention from their nearest parent (schema → database → account) if not explicitly set. Since the database has 10 days and the table has no override, the table inherits 10 days.

text: Which TWO objects can be restored using UNDROP? (Select TWO)

options.A: Tables
options.B: Warehouses
options.C: Schemas
options.D: Stages

explanation: UNDROP works for: tables, schemas, databases, tags, external volumes, and accounts. It does NOT work for: warehouses, stages, pipes, views, or streams.

text: A cloned table is created: CREATE TABLE orders_clone CLONE orders. How much additional storage does the clone immediately consume?

options.A: The same size as the original table
options.B: Zero additional storage — zero-copy cloning shares the same micro-partitions until data diverges
options.C: 50% of the original (compressed reference)
options.D: Depends on the number of columns

explanation: Zero-copy cloning creates a metadata reference to the same underlying micro-partitions. No additional storage is consumed until data in the clone diverges from the original (via INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE).

text: Which TWO objects CANNOT be cloned? (Select TWO)

options.A: Permanent tables
options.B: Internal (Snowflake) stages
options.C: Schemas
options.D: External tables

explanation: Cannot be cloned: internal stages, external tables, dynamic tables, pipes, shares, warehouses. CAN be cloned: tables (permanent/transient/temporary), schemas, databases, external stages (metadata only).

text: A table has a column with a DEFAULT value from a sequence. The table is cloned. What happens to the sequence reference in the clone?

options.A: The clone creates a new independent sequence
options.B: The clone references the SAME original sequence — it is NOT duplicated
options.C: The clone loses the default value entirely
options.D: The sequence values reset to 1 in the clone

explanation: Cloning does NOT duplicate sequences. The cloned table's DEFAULT still references the original sequence. Both tables share the same sequence, which may lead to unexpected gaps or conflicts if both are actively inserting.

text: What is the difference between a replication group and a failover group?

options.A: They are identical — just different names
options.B: A replication group provides read-only replicas. A failover group extends this with read-WRITE failover capability.
options.C: A failover group only replicates databases; a replication group replicates all objects
options.D: A replication group requires VPS edition

explanation: Replication group: read-only secondary copies. Failover group: extends replication with the ability to promote a secondary to primary (read-write) for disaster recovery. Failover groups require Business Critical Edition+.

text: Can replication work across different cloud platforms (e.g., AWS to Azure)?

options.A: No — replication only works within the same cloud
options.B: Yes — replication works cross-region AND cross-cloud within the same Snowflake organization
options.C: Yes, but only for databases (not other objects)
options.D: Yes, but only with VPS edition

explanation: Snowflake replication supports cross-region AND cross-cloud replication within the same organization. You can replicate from AWS to Azure or GCP. Database and share replication is available on all editions; other object types require Business Critical+.

text: Which Snowflake edition is required for failover groups (read-write failover)?

options.A: Standard Edition
options.B: Enterprise Edition
options.C: Business Critical Edition or higher
options.D: Any edition

explanation: Failover groups (with read-write promotion capability) require Business Critical Edition or higher. Database and share replication groups (read-only) are available on all editions.

text: A provider creates a direct share and adds a consumer account in a different region. What happens?

options.A: The share works — direct shares support cross-region access
options.B: The share FAILS — direct shares only work within the SAME region. Use Listings for cross-region sharing.
options.C: The share works but with a 24-hour replication delay
options.D: The share works but incurs data transfer charges

explanation: Direct shares only work within the same Snowflake region. For cross-region (or cross-cloud) sharing, use Listings with Auto-Fulfillment, which automatically replicates data to the consumer's region.

text: A consumer receives a share and tries to INSERT a row into a shared table. What happens?

options.A: The INSERT succeeds — consumers can modify shared data
options.B: The INSERT FAILS — shared data is READ-ONLY for consumers. They cannot INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or CLONE.
options.C: The INSERT succeeds but is logged as unauthorized
options.D: The INSERT is queued for provider approval

explanation: Shared objects are strictly read-only for consumers. No DML (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE) or CLONE is possible. To get a writable copy, the consumer must CREATE TABLE AS SELECT from the shared data.

text: A provider drops a table that is included in a share. What happens on the consumer side?

options.A: The consumer retains a cached copy of the data
options.B: The table becomes immediately inaccessible to the consumer — no cached copy exists
options.C: The consumer is notified 24 hours in advance
options.D: The consumer's database is dropped automatically

explanation: Shared data is accessed in real-time from the provider. If the provider drops a shared object, it is immediately inaccessible to the consumer. There is no cached copy. The consumer's database shell remains but the object is gone.

text: Which type of view can be added to a share?

options.A: Standard view
options.B: Secure view — only secure views can be shared because they hide the view definition
options.C: Materialized view
options.D: Any view type

explanation: Only SECURE views (and secure UDFs) can be added to shares. Standard views expose their SQL definition, which is a security risk. Materialized views cannot be shared directly.

text: Who pays for the compute when a consumer queries shared data via a direct share?

options.A: The provider pays for all consumer compute
options.B: The CONSUMER pays — they use their own warehouse to query shared data
options.C: Snowflake absorbs the compute cost
options.D: Costs are split 50/50

explanation: With direct shares, the consumer uses their OWN warehouse to query shared data. The provider incurs no compute cost — only their storage. This is different from Reader Accounts where the provider pays.

text: A Reader Account is created for a business partner who doesn't have their own Snowflake account. Who pays for the Reader Account's warehouse usage?

options.A: The business partner (Reader Account owner)
options.B: The PROVIDER pays for ALL compute — Reader Accounts are billed entirely to the creating provider
options.C: Snowflake covers Reader Account costs
options.D: No charges — Reader Accounts are free

explanation: Reader Accounts: the PROVIDER pays for all compute (warehouse credits). The provider creates and manages the Reader Account. This is the key cost distinction vs. regular consumer accounts.

text: Which role is required to create a Reader Account?

options.A: SYSADMIN
options.B: SECURITYADMIN
options.C: ACCOUNTADMIN
options.D: USERADMIN

explanation: ACCOUNTADMIN is required to create a Reader Account. This is non-delegable by default. Reader Accounts are managed consumer accounts for partners without their own Snowflake subscription.

text: Which TWO statements about Reader Accounts are TRUE? (Select TWO)

options.A: Reader Accounts cannot create warehouses
options.B: Reader Accounts CAN create warehouses, databases, schemas, tables, and views
options.C: Provider pays for all Reader Account compute
options.D: Reader Accounts can access the Snowflake Marketplace

explanation: Reader Accounts CAN create objects (warehouses, databases, tables, views) for joining with shared data. Provider pays ALL compute. They CANNOT: create shares, create pipes/stages, or access the Marketplace.

text: A provider adds a new column to a shared table. Does the consumer need to do anything to see it?

options.A: The consumer must refresh their database from the share
options.B: No action needed — schema changes are automatically visible to consumers immediately
options.C: The consumer must re-create the database from the share
options.D: The consumer must request access to the new column

explanation: Schema changes (new columns, new tables added to the share) are automatically and immediately visible to consumers. No refresh, re-creation, or additional grants are needed.

text: Can a consumer clone a shared table?

options.A: Yes — cloning works on any visible table
options.B: No — the consumer cannot clone shared objects because they do not have OWNERSHIP on them
options.C: Yes, but only with ACCOUNTADMIN role
options.D: Yes, but it creates a read-only copy

explanation: Cloning requires OWNERSHIP privilege on the object. Consumers have IMPORTED PRIVILEGES (read-only) on shared objects, not OWNERSHIP. To copy data, they must use CREATE TABLE AS SELECT.

text: What is a Data Clean Room in Snowflake?

options.A: A data sanitization pipeline that removes PII
options.B: A secure environment where multiple parties collaborate using pre-approved query templates without seeing each other's raw data
options.C: A staging area for data validation before loading
options.D: An encrypted database for healthcare data

explanation: Data Clean Rooms enable multi-party collaboration with privacy controls. Pre-approved query templates define what analysis can be performed. Neither party sees the other's raw data — only aggregated or approved results.

text: What is the key difference between a direct share and a Listing?

options.A: Listings are free; direct shares cost money
options.B: Direct shares work same-region only. Listings support cross-region (via Auto-Fulfillment), monetization, and Marketplace discovery.
options.C: Direct shares support more object types than Listings
options.D: Listings are real-time; direct shares have latency

explanation: Direct shares: same-region only, no monetization, no discovery. Listings: cross-region (Auto-Fulfillment replicates), optional monetization, discoverable on Marketplace. Listings are the modern approach.

text: A provider wants to make their data publicly available to ALL Snowflake customers. What type of listing should they create?

options.A: Private listing — targeted to specific accounts
options.B: Public listing on the Snowflake Marketplace — visible to all customers after Snowflake review
options.C: Direct share to all accounts in the organization
options.D: Reader Account for each interested customer

explanation: Public listings on the Snowflake Marketplace are visible to all Snowflake customers. They require Snowflake review before becoming visible. Private listings target specific invited accounts and are immediately available.

text: A consumer wants to install a Marketplace listing. Which privilege do they need?

options.A: CREATE SHARE
options.B: IMPORT SHARE — required to get/install listings from the Marketplace
options.C: CREATE DATABASE only
options.D: ACCOUNTADMIN role (no specific privilege)

explanation: IMPORT SHARE is the privilege required to get/install listings from the Snowflake Marketplace. The consumer also needs CREATE DATABASE to create the database from the listing.

text: A Native App is installed by a consumer from the Marketplace. Whose compute resources does the app run on?

options.A: The provider's compute — billed back to them
options.B: The CONSUMER's compute — Native Apps run on consumer infrastructure
options.C: Shared serverless compute managed by Snowflake
options.D: Dedicated Marketplace infrastructure

explanation: Native Apps run on the CONSUMER's compute resources. The provider packages code + data, but runtime costs are borne by the consumer. This is a fundamental design principle — providers don't pay for consumer compute.

text: A public listing is submitted to the Snowflake Marketplace. Is it immediately visible to all customers?

options.A: Yes — public listings are immediately live
options.B: No — Snowflake reviews public listings before they become visible. Only private listings are immediate.
options.C: Yes, but only in the provider's region
options.D: No — it takes 7 days for automatic approval

explanation: Public Marketplace listings require Snowflake review/approval before becoming visible. This ensures quality and compliance. Private listings (shared to specific accounts) are available immediately.

text: An engineer clones a database. Are the grants on objects inside the database (tables, views) preserved in the clone?

options.A: No — all grants are stripped from the clone
options.B: Yes — grants on objects WITHIN the cloned container ARE preserved. Grants on the container itself are NOT.
options.C: Only OWNERSHIP grants are preserved
options.D: All grants including container-level are fully copied

explanation: When cloning a database/schema: privileges on the CONTAINER (database/schema itself) do NOT transfer. But privileges on objects INSIDE (tables, views, etc.) ARE preserved. Internal access structure is maintained.

text: Can database roles be shared via shares?

options.A: No — only tables and secure views can be shared
options.B: Yes — database roles can be included in shares, enabling fine-grained access control for consumers
options.C: Yes, but only with VPS edition
options.D: No — roles are account-level objects and cannot be shared

explanation: Database roles (scoped to a single database) can be shared via shares. This enables providers to define fine-grained access control that consumers grant to their own account roles. Account roles cannot be shared.

text: A DML operation runs concurrently with a CLONE command on the same table. Does the DML affect the clone?

options.A: Yes — the clone includes the concurrent DML changes
options.B: No — cloning captures a transactional snapshot. Concurrent DML does NOT affect the clone.
options.C: The clone operation fails due to the concurrent DML
options.D: It depends on which started first

explanation: Cloning captures a consistent transactional snapshot at the moment the CLONE statement is processed. Concurrent DML operations do not affect or corrupt the cloned data.

text: Storage billing for a table includes which components?

options.A: Active data only
options.B: Active data + Time Travel data + Fail-safe data (all billed based on monthly average bytes)
options.C: Active data + Time Travel only
options.D: Only data accessed in the last 30 days

explanation: Storage billing = active data + Time Travel data + Fail-safe data. All three components are billed based on average monthly bytes stored. Dropping data doesn't immediately reduce costs due to Time Travel + Fail-safe retention.

text: A provider has a share with active consumers. They revoke the share. What happens to the consumer's database?

options.A: The consumer's database and all data are completely deleted
options.B: The consumer's database shell REMAINS but all shared objects become inaccessible (empty database)
options.C: Nothing changes — the consumer retains a full copy
options.D: The database is frozen for 30 days then deleted

explanation: When a provider revokes a share, the consumer's database FROM SHARE remains as an empty shell — it is not automatically dropped. But all shared objects within it become inaccessible immediately.

text: Standard Edition supports a maximum Time Travel retention of how many days?

options.A: 0 or 1 day only
options.B: Up to 30 days
options.C: Up to 90 days
options.D: No Time Travel on Standard

explanation: Standard Edition: 0 or 1 day Time Travel (configurable). Enterprise Edition+: 0 to 90 days for permanent tables. Transient/temporary tables: always 0 or 1 day regardless of edition.

text: A Listing uses Auto-Fulfillment to serve consumers in a different region. Does this incur additional storage costs?

options.A: No — zero-copy sharing works cross-region
options.B: Yes — Auto-Fulfillment REPLICATES data to the consumer's region, incurring storage costs for the replicated copy
options.C: No — only network egress costs apply
options.D: Yes, but only for paid listings

explanation: Auto-Fulfillment replicates data to the consumer's region. Unlike direct shares (zero-copy, same region), cross-region Auto-Fulfillment creates a replicated copy, incurring storage and compute costs for the replication.

text: Which TWO objects CANNOT be added to a share? (Select TWO)

options.A: Tables
options.B: Stored procedures
options.C: Secure views
options.D: Warehouses

explanation: Cannot be shared: stored procedures, warehouses, stages, materialized views (non-secure), standard views. CAN be shared: tables, secure views, secure UDFs, external tables, database roles.

text: An engineer drops a schema that contains tables with 30-day Time Travel. The schema itself has 1-day retention. How long is the schema (and its tables) available for UNDROP?

options.A: 30 days (tables have longer retention)
options.B: 1 day — when a container is dropped, child objects inherit the CONTAINER's retention, not their own
options.C: 37 days (30 + 7 Fail-safe)
options.D: The longer of the two (30 days)

explanation: When a container (database/schema) is dropped, child objects inherit the container's retention period regardless of their own explicit settings. To honor child retention, drop child objects individually BEFORE dropping the container.

text: Which ACCOUNT_USAGE view tracks how consumers use monetized Marketplace listings?

options.A: SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY
options.B: SNOWFLAKE.DATA_SHARING_USAGE.MONETIZED_USAGE_DAILY
options.C: SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY
options.D: SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.LOGIN_HISTORY

explanation: MONETIZED_USAGE_DAILY (in DATA_SHARING_USAGE schema) tracks usage of monetized Marketplace listings. LISTING_TELEMETRY_DAILY tracks listing views/access. These are separate from standard ACCOUNT_USAGE views.

text: What objects can be replicated in a replication group? (Select the MOST complete answer)

options.A: Databases only
options.B: Databases and shares only
options.C: Databases, shares, roles, users, warehouses, network policies, integrations, and resource monitors
options.D: Only tables and views within databases

explanation: Replication groups can include: databases, shares, roles, users, warehouses, resource monitors, integrations, network policies, and account parameters. Database and share replication is available on all editions; other object types require Business Critical+.
